Inverse probability weighting with ipw

Source: vignettes/ipw.Rmd
ipw.Rmd
library(ipw)
library(survival)

ipw estimates inverse probability weights: each person is weighted by the inverse of the probability of the exposure they actually received, given their confounders. In the weighted data, exposure no longer depends on the measured confounders, and a simple model of outcome on exposure, a marginal structural model (MSM), estimates the causal effect (Robins, Hernán & Brumback 2000; van der Wal & Geskus 2011).

An analysis has three steps:

  1. Estimate the weights with ipwpoint() (exposure measured once) or ipwtm() (exposure that changes over time), or from your own probabilities with ipwprob().
  2. Check the weights with summary() and ipwplot().
  3. Fit the MSM with the weights, and get standard errors, preferably with ipwboot().
Function Purpose
ipwpoint() Weights for an exposure measured once (point treatment)
ipwtm() Weights for an exposure that changes over time, and censoring weights
ipwprob() Weights from probabilities you estimated yourself (new)
ipwboot() Bootstrap standard errors that re-estimate the weights (new)
ipwplot() Plot the distribution of the weights
tstartfun() Interval start times for counting-process (Cox) data

New in the development version. Sections marked New describe features added after ipw 1.3.2: count, gamma and log-normal exposures, smooth terms with mgcv, ATT and overlap weights, type = "all" for categorical and survival exposures in ipwtm(), ipwprob() and ipwboot(). Existing calls give the same results as before.

1. Point treatment: a binary exposure

We simulate a confounder l, a binary exposure a that is more likely at high l, and an outcome y. The true causal effect of a on y is 10.

set.seed(16)
n <- 1000
simdat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n, 10, 5))
simdat$a <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(simdat$l - 10))
simdat$y <- 10 * simdat$a + 0.5 * simdat$l + rnorm(n, -10, 5)

ipwpoint() fits the exposure model (here a logistic regression) and returns the weights. With numerator = ~ 1 the weights are stabilized: the marginal probability of the exposure goes in the numerator, which keeps the correction but makes the weights much less variable.

w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
              numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = simdat)
summary(w$ipw.weights)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.4810  0.5127  0.5285  0.9095  0.6318 74.6994
ipwplot(weights = w$ipw.weights, logscale = FALSE, main = "Stabilized weights",
        xlim = c(0, 8))

Stabilized weights should have a mean close to 1. The exposure models are returned as well, so they can be checked like any regression:

coef(w$den.mod)
#> (Intercept)           l 
#>  -9.6980874   0.9727157

The weighted regression of y on a estimates the causal effect; the unweighted regression is confounded by l:

c(unweighted = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat))["a"]),
  weighted   = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w$ipw.weights))["a"]))
#> unweighted   weighted 
#>   13.87050   10.64661

For inference, the weighted model is usually fitted with robust standard errors, for example with the survey package as in the JSS paper; see section 7 for why the bootstrap is better.

msm <- survey::svyglm(y ~ a, design = survey::svydesign(~ 1, weights = ~ w$ipw.weights,
                                                        data = simdat))
cbind(estimate = coef(msm), confint(msm))["a", ]
#>  estimate     2.5 %    97.5 % 
#> 10.646610  8.311695 12.981525

Unstabilized weights use numerator = NULL (the default), and truncation caps extreme weights at chosen percentiles:

w.unstab <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                     denominator = ~ l, data = simdat)
w.trunc <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                    numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, trunc = 0.01)
rbind(unstabilized = summary(w.unstab$ipw.weights),
      stabilized   = summary(w$ipw.weights),
      truncated    = summary(w.trunc$weights.trunc))
#>                   Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean  3rd Qu.       Max.
#> unstabilized 1.0000000 1.0046903 1.0482683 1.8260844 1.242464 155.300216
#> stabilized   0.4810000 0.5127181 0.5284768 0.9094652 0.631794  74.699404
#> truncated    0.4810092 0.5127181 0.5284768 0.7772294 0.631794   6.274768

New: ATT and overlap weights

The weights above target the average treatment effect (ATE): the effect if everyone versus no one were exposed. With estimand = "ATT" the weights target the effect in the exposed (exposed get weight 1, unexposed p/(1 - p)); with estimand = "ATO", overlap weights, the effect in the people whose exposure was most uncertain (exposed 1 - p, unexposed p, all between 0 and 1). Here p is the fitted probability of exposure.

fit.estimand <- function(estimand) {
  wt <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                 denominator = ~ l, data = simdat, estimand = estimand)$ipw.weights
  c(effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = wt))["a"]),
    max.weight = max(wt))
}
sapply(c(ATE = "ATE", ATT = "ATT", ATO = "ATO"), fit.estimand)
#>                  ATE        ATT        ATO
#> effect      10.64661   9.044102 10.5137145
#> max.weight 155.30022 154.300216  0.9935609

The effect was simulated as constant, so all three estimands are 10 in truth, and the differences between the estimates are sampling noise. The ATT weights show why: unexposed people with a high probability of exposure get weights above 100, which makes that estimate unstable. Overlap weights never exceed 1, which helps when some people are almost always or almost never exposed. With an effect that differs between people, the three estimands differ in truth as well.

2. Point treatment: other kinds of exposure

Categorical and ordered exposures

For an exposure with more than two categories, family = "multinomial" fits a multinomial logistic model and family = "ordinal" a proportional-odds model (with link = "logit", "probit", "cauchit" or "cloglog").

set.seed(4)
cat.dat <- data.frame(l = rnorm(800))
eta <- 0.9 * cat.dat$l
cat.dat$dose <- cut(eta + rlogis(800), c(-Inf, -0.5, 0.8, Inf),
                    labels = c("low", "medium", "high"), ordered_result = TRUE)
w.ord <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cat.dat)
w.mult <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "multinomial",
                   numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cat.dat)
rbind(ordinal = summary(w.ord$ipw.weights), multinomial = summary(w.mult$ipw.weights))
#>                  Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
#> ordinal     0.3728385 0.7198835 0.8864612 0.9986363 1.095597 5.308914
#> multinomial 0.3563447 0.7223290 0.8959666 1.0031794 1.063840 7.484257

Continuous exposures

healthdat contains IQ, monthly income and a health score for 1000 simulated people; IQ confounds the effect of income on health. For a continuous exposure the weights use densities instead of probabilities, so a numerator model is required.

data(healthdat)
w.gauss <- ipwpoint(exposure = income, family = "gaussian",
                    numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ iq, data = healthdat)
summary(w.gauss$ipw.weights)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#>  0.01669  0.55729  0.72481  0.96870  0.93367 58.09496
coef(lm(health ~ income, data = healthdat, weights = w.gauss$ipw.weights))
#>  (Intercept)       income 
#> 47.167435110  0.008022911

New: skewed continuous exposures (gamma and log-normal)

Many exposures are positive with a long right tail, such as a dose or a duration: most values are small and a few are very large. A normal model is symmetric and fits that tail poorly, and the tail is where weights become large. family = "gamma" (log link) and family = "lognormal" (a normal model for the log of the exposure) are meant for such exposures; both require positive values. Below, the dose is log-normal given l, and the true effect of one unit of dose on y is 1.

set.seed(8)
n.sk <- 2000
sk <- data.frame(l = rnorm(n.sk))
sk$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * sk$l + rnorm(n.sk, 0, 0.6))
sk$y <- sk$dose + 2 * sk$l + rnorm(n.sk)
c(mean = mean(sk$dose), median = median(sk$dose))   # right-skewed
#>     mean   median 
#> 2.311130 1.655365

# weighted correlation of the dose (or log dose) with the confounder l
wcor <- function(x, w) cov.wt(cbind(x, sk$l), wt = w, cor = TRUE)$cor[1, 2]

fit.dose <- function(family) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = family, numerator = ~ 1,
                denominator = ~ l, data = sk, trunc = 0.01)
  wt <- w$weights.trunc
  c(cor.dose.l = wcor(sk$dose, wt), cor.logdose.l = wcor(log(sk$dose), wt),
    effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ dose, data = sk, weights = wt))["dose"]),
    max.weight.untruncated = max(w$ipw.weights))
}
round(cbind(
  unweighted = c(wcor(sk$dose, rep(1, n.sk)), wcor(log(sk$dose), rep(1, n.sk)),
                 unname(coef(lm(y ~ dose, data = sk))["dose"]), 1),
  sapply(c(gaussian = "gaussian", gamma = "gamma", lognormal = "lognormal"), fit.dose)), 3)
#>                        unweighted gaussian   gamma lognormal
#> cor.dose.l                  0.564    0.333   0.256     0.171
#> cor.logdose.l               0.649    0.441   0.320     0.185
#> effect                      1.529    1.265   1.244     1.172
#> max.weight.untruncated      1.000 1825.069 491.946    37.537

Good weights make the exposure unrelated to the confounders, so the table shows the weighted correlation of the dose (and of the log dose) with l, next to the effect estimate and the largest weight. The weights are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles (trunc = 0.01), because a few extreme weights would otherwise dominate a single estimate.

Without weights, the dose is strongly correlated with l (about 0.56) and the estimate (about 1.53) is badly confounded. The log-normal model, which matches how the dose was generated, removes most of that correlation (about 0.17), gives the estimate closest to 1 (about 1.17) and has by far the most moderate weights: its largest untruncated weight is about 38, against about 1800 for the gaussian model. The gaussian model puts almost no probability on the long right tail, so the few people with a high dose get huge weights; the gamma model lies in between. None of the models removes the correlation completely here, partly because truncation trades a little bias for stability.

Choose the family by looking at the exposure: if it is right-skewed and looks bell-shaped after taking logs, use "lognormal"; if its spread grows with its mean, "gamma". Do not use them for an exposure that is roughly symmetric: income in healthdat (mean and median both about 2700) is modelled well by "gaussian", and a log-normal model there gives a few people with very low income enormous weights.

New: count exposures (Poisson and negative binomial)

For counts, such as a number of visits, family = "poisson" fits a Poisson model and family = "negbin" a negative binomial model (via MASS::glm.nb) that allows more spread than the Poisson. Here the true effect of each extra visit on y is 0.5.

set.seed(6)
cnt <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
cnt$visits <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * cnt$l))
cnt$y <- 0.5 * cnt$visits + cnt$l + rnorm(1000)
c(mean = mean(cnt$visits), variance = var(cnt$visits))   # variance > mean
#>     mean variance 
#> 1.853000 4.483875
w.pois <- ipwpoint(exposure = visits, family = "poisson",
                   numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cnt)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = visits, family = "negbin",
                 numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = cnt)
sapply(list(poisson = w.pois, negbin = w.nb), function(x)
  c(effect = unname(coef(lm(y ~ visits, data = cnt, weights = x$ipw.weights))["visits"]),
    max.weight = max(x$ipw.weights)))
#>               poisson    negbin
#> effect      0.3779291 0.5500115
#> max.weight 20.1565447 5.9796435

The variance is clearly larger than the mean, so the negative binomial model is the better choice for these data.

New: smooth terms with mgcv

A regression assumes a straight-line effect of each confounder on the logit of the exposure probability. When the true relation is curved, the weights leave residual confounding. Writing s(l) in a formula fits the exposure model as a generalized additive model with mgcv, which estimates the shape of the curve from the data. Smooth terms work in ipwpoint() for the binomial, gaussian and Poisson families and in ipwtm() for the binomial family. The true effect below is 2.

set.seed(10)
nl <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
nl$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * nl$l)))
nl$y <- 2 * nl$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * nl$l) + rnorm(2000)

w.lin <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = nl)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = nl)
c(unweighted   = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl))["a"]),
  linear.model = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl, weights = w.lin$ipw.weights))["a"]),
  smooth.model = unname(coef(lm(y ~ a, data = nl, weights = w.gam$ipw.weights))["a"]))
#>   unweighted linear.model smooth.model 
#>     4.437406     2.682710     2.084703

plot(w.gam$den.mod) shows the fitted curve. A covariate that is simply named s, te, ti or t2 is treated as an ordinary variable.

3. Exposure that changes over time

HAART and mortality (haartdat)

haartdat contains simulated follow-up of 1200 HIV-infected patients from seroconversion, one row per 100 days. Patients can start HAART (haartind becomes 1 and stays 1). CD4 count is a time-varying confounder: low CD4 leads to starting HAART and to death, and HAART raises CD4. Ordinary adjustment for CD4 would remove part of the effect of HAART; weighting does not.

data(haartdat)
head(haartdat[, c("patient", "tstart", "fuptime", "haartind", "event", "cd4.sqrt", "dropout")])
#>   patient tstart fuptime haartind event cd4.sqrt dropout
#> 1       1   -100       0        0     0 23.83275       0
#> 2       1      0     100        0     0 25.59297       0
#> 3       1    100     200        0     0 23.47339       0
#> 4       1    200     300        0     0 24.16609       0
#> 5       1    300     400        0     0 23.23790       0
#> 6       1    400     500        0     0 24.85961       0

ipwtm() with family = "survival" fits Cox models for the time to starting HAART. With type = "first", each patient contributes until HAART is started, because afterwards starting is no longer a choice. A second set of weights corrects for informative censoring: dropout also depends on CD4.

w.haart <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival",
                 numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                 id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                 type = "first", data = haartdat)
w.cens <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival",
                numerator = ~ sex + age, denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt,
                id = patient, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                type = "cens", data = haartdat)
summary(w.haart$ipw.weights * w.cens$ipw.weights)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.2500  0.8944  0.9862  1.0346  1.0718  7.0921
ipwplot(weights = w.haart$ipw.weights, timevar = haartdat$fuptime, binwidth = 100,
        main = "Stabilized weights for starting HAART")

The MSM is a weighted Cox model for death with the product of the two weights:

msm.haart <- coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind + cluster(patient),
                   data = haartdat, weights = w.haart$ipw.weights * w.cens$ipw.weights)
summary(msm.haart)$conf.int
#>          exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
#> haartind 0.3920629   2.550611 0.1614445 0.9521124

tstartfun() builds the interval start times needed for such data from the end times:

toy <- data.frame(patient = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2), time = c(14, 34, 41, 0, 11))
toy$tstart <- tstartfun(patient, time, toy)
toy
#>   patient time tstart
#> 1       1   14     -1
#> 2       1   34     14
#> 3       1   41     34
#> 4       2    0     -1
#> 5       2   11      0

Other families work in ipwtm() as well: "binomial" (pooled logistic regression), "multinomial", "ordinal" and "gaussian" (GEE, with type = "all").

New: categorical exposures that switch back and forth

With type = "all", every interval contributes the probability of the category observed in it, so an exposure can move between categories in both directions. This now works for multinomial and ordinal exposures. The models are pooled over time, so past exposure belongs in the formulas; here the previous dose level dose.lag.

set.seed(3)
n.id <- 300
long <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(n.id), each = 4), time = rep(1:4, times = n.id))
long$l <- rnorm(nrow(long))
long$dose <- NA
long$dose.lag <- NA
for (t in 1:4) {
  rows <- long$time == t
  prev <- if (t == 1) rep(1, n.id) else long$dose[long$time == t - 1]
  eta <- -1 + 0.8 * long$l[rows] + 0.7 * (prev - 1)
  u <- runif(n.id)
  long$dose.lag[rows] <- prev
  long$dose[rows] <- ifelse(u < plogis(eta - 1.5), 3, ifelse(u < plogis(eta), 2, 1))
}
long$dose <- factor(long$dose, levels = 1:3, labels = c("low", "medium", "high"),
                    ordered = TRUE)

w.dose <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
                numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
                id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
summary(w.dose$ipw.weights)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.1015  0.6728  0.8916  1.0009  1.1278  6.3704
ipwplot(weights = w.dose$ipw.weights, timevar = long$time, binwidth = 1,
        main = "Cumulative stabilized weights by visit")

New: recurrent exposure events in survival models

family = "survival" previously allowed only type = "first". With type = "all" (Graffeo, Latouche, Geskus & Chevret 2018), the exposure indicator marks an exposure event at the end of an interval, such as a new prescription, that may happen more than once per person. An Andersen-Gill Cox model is fitted on all rows, and each row contributes the probability of the observed status over its own interval. The intervals may be irregular and differ between people.

set.seed(21)
n.id <- 300
rec <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(n.id), function(i) {
  k <- sample(3:6, 1)
  cuts <- sort(runif(k))
  data.frame(id = i, tstart = c(0, cuts[-k]), fuptime = cuts)
}))
rec$x <- rep(rbinom(n.id, 1, 0.5), times = as.vector(table(rec$id)))  # fixed covariate
rec$xt <- rbinom(nrow(rec), 1, 0.4)                                    # time-varying
rec$expo <- rbinom(nrow(rec), 1, plogis(-1 + 0.5 * rec$x - rec$xt))   # exposure events

w.first <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ x,
                 denominator = ~ x + xt, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
                 type = "first", data = rec)
w.all <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ x,
               denominator = ~ x + xt, id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime,
               type = "all", data = rec)
c(rows.used.first = sum(w.first$selvar), rows.used.all = sum(w.all$selvar))
#> rows.used.first   rows.used.all 
#>             832            1376
rbind(first = summary(w.first$ipw.weights), all = summary(w.all$ipw.weights))
#>            Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
#> first 0.7480747 0.8333341 1.0000000 0.9908948 1.000000 1.435220
#> all   0.3741005 0.8114862 0.9444067 0.9815656 1.087444 2.394201

With type = "first", the rows after a person’s first exposure event are ignored; with type = "all" they all count. For a treatment that is started and stopped, Graffeo et al. compute weights separately for starting (on the rows off treatment) and for stopping (on the rows on treatment).

4. New: weights from your own probabilities

ipwprob() turns probabilities you estimated yourself, for example with a machine-learning model or SuperLearner, into weights. Give the probability (or density) of the exposure each person actually received; with id and timevar, the ratios are multiplied over time within each person. Below, a cubic logistic model stands in for a flexible learner.

p.flex <- fitted(glm(a ~ poly(l, 3), family = binomial, data = simdat))
#> Warning: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred
w.own <- ipwprob(den = ifelse(simdat$a == 1, p.flex, 1 - p.flex),
                 num = ifelse(simdat$a == 1, mean(simdat$a), 1 - mean(simdat$a)))
summary(w.own$ipw.weights)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.4810  0.5095  0.5301  0.8856  0.6332 58.5053
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = simdat, weights = w.own$ipw.weights))["a"]
#>        a 
#> 10.92033

# time-varying: ratios multiplied within each person, in time order
toy <- data.frame(id = c(1, 1, 2, 2), time = c(1, 2, 1, 2), p = c(0.5, 0.8, 0.4, 0.9))
ipwprob(den = toy$p, id = toy$id, timevar = toy$time)$ipw.weights
#> [1] 2.000000 2.500000 2.500000 2.777778

The warning from glm() is a reminder of the main risk: flexible models can produce probabilities close to 0 or 1 and therefore extreme weights. Check the weights and consider trunc.

5. New: bootstrap standard errors with ipwboot()

Robust (sandwich) standard errors treat the weights as known. In simulations of weighted Cox models, Austin (2016) found naive standard errors too small and robust standard errors too large; only the bootstrap that re-estimates the weights in each bootstrap sample gave correct standard errors and confidence intervals.

ipwboot() does the resampling. You write a function that takes a data set and returns the estimate, computing the weights itself:

msm.effect <- function(d) {
  wt <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                 numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = wt))["a"]
}
set.seed(1)
boot.point <- ipwboot(simdat, msm.effect, R = 200)
boot.point
#> Bootstrap of an inverse probability weighted analysis
#> 200 bootstrap samples, resampling rows
#> 
#>   estimate    se 2.5 % 97.5 %
#> a    10.65 1.114 8.867  12.85
confint(boot.point, level = 0.90)
#>        5 %     95 %
#> a 9.122687 12.63303

For data with several rows per person, give id: whole people are resampled with all their rows, and each sampled copy gets a new identifier, so someone drawn twice counts as two people. Here both sets of weights for the HAART example are re-estimated in each sample (use about 200 samples in practice; 20 keep this vignette quick):

haart.effect <- function(d) {
  w1 <- ipwtm(exposure = haartind, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "first", data = d)
  w2 <- ipwtm(exposure = dropout, family = "survival", numerator = ~ sex + age,
              denominator = ~ sex + age + cd4.sqrt, id = patient,
              tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "cens", data = d)
  coef(coxph(Surv(tstart, fuptime, event) ~ haartind, data = d,
             weights = w1$ipw.weights * w2$ipw.weights))
}
set.seed(2)
boot.haart <- ipwboot(haartdat, haart.effect, id = patient, R = 20)
boot.haart
#> Bootstrap of an inverse probability weighted analysis
#> 20 bootstrap samples, resampling subjects ('patient')
#> 
#>          estimate    se  2.5 %  97.5 %
#> haartind  -0.9363 0.362 -1.495 -0.2691
c(robust.se = unname(sqrt(diag(vcov(msm.haart)))), bootstrap.se = unname(boot.haart$se))
#>    robust.se bootstrap.se 
#>    0.4526924    0.3620001

ipwboot() also supports strata (resampling within groups) and records samples in which the analysis fails instead of stopping. Set a seed with set.seed() for reproducible results.

6. Checking the weights

  • Mean close to 1. Stabilized weights should average about 1; a mean far from 1 suggests a misspecified exposure model.
  • Extreme weights. Very large weights point to positivity problems: some kinds of people (almost) never receive one of the exposures. Look at ipwplot(), reconsider the model, use overlap weights (estimand = "ATO") or truncate (trunc), keeping in mind that truncation slightly changes what is estimated.
  • Assumptions. The weighted analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding, positivity, consistency and correctly specified exposure (and censoring) models.

References
